doc.title: Howard Levy interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 11, 2025

title: Writing the concerto and improvisation in classical music
summary: Levy explains he wrote the concerto with improvised sections, and argues classical composers were improvisers.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Listening to classical music, then and now

blocks.x: Not really. It’s a funny thing how that concerto came about but I wrote it as a commission for an orchestra in Chicago. And I never studied composition, I never studied orchestration. And I just had to do it myself. And so I did. I wrote it out in pencil and then I gave it to a copyist and they made parts and made a score and everything. And the first time I performed it I was kind of terrified in certain ways because I also left room for myself to improvise in each movement. The first movement has a big cadenza, and the second movement I actually blow over those changes of that melody that you were playing. And the third movement also has a section that I left myself room to improvise over what are basically the changes of the Paganini solo violin “Caprice #24.” Because you know in getting into classical music, which I really got deeply into for a while right around when I was writing this piece and studying the lives of the composers, all those guys were jazz musicians. They were all improvisers. Every last one of them was an improviser. But if you wanted people to hear your solos you had to write them down. I mean it’s like a fact. Beethoven could improvise a fucking sonata. He did that for someone once and they thought he was lying. He just improvised it. Bach, you could whistle him a tune and he could improvise on it for an hour and a half. He could improvise fugues and canons and stuff. I mean all these guys were just – the improvisational element in classical music had to be written down, but they all left room for cadenzas and concertos they wrote for themselves, and they wrote for others too. And so I thought well of course I have to leave some room to blow. And I mean there are stories about Mozart taking requests from audiences in concerts. Like, “Play that aria from your opera.” And he’d sit down and if he was in a real good mood he would just improvise something. And if he liked it he’d go home and write it out.

It’s like yeah, I mean all those guys. They had just colossal brain power and colossal ears and you know we’re spoiled because jazz spread through sound, through sound reproduction. And everyone said, “Oh let’s get the latest Bird album, let’s get the latest Coltrane album, let’s listen to this and figure this out.” Back then there were no albums. I mean you had to go hear someone play or get a score and study it. And that’s what all those guys did. They all studied scores and Bach, I think he walked for like two weeks to hear this one organist play – I can’t remember the story. But yeah. I mean they were much more similar to us than different. And classical music just got kind of fossilized in a certain way because the repertoire started growing so huge that classical musicians, the idea of improvising was like yeah, just figure out how to play Schoenberg and Tchaikovsky and Brahms and Bach and Vivaldi, all the things that you had to do if you’re in an orchestra or a string quartet, when do you have time to improvise? You know? And so the classical players who back in the day, they were improvising all the time and the keyboard players like Bach would write out those figured bass keyboard parts, and all it was, it was the bass line and the changes.
Yeah. He was writing chord changes.

And of course all these keyboard players knew how to do that because that’s what you did. Like give us a lead sheet, yeah. I’d much rather see a lead sheet than someone write out chord voicings, I’d be sitting there going [grunts] and getting behind. So they were way more similar to us than they were different. And so I try to have some of that spirit in my concerto you know.
